Investment memo · MAERSK.B-DK · 13 November 2026

Maersk: earnings are heading into a long freight-rate trough that the shares have not yet priced, so the opportunity to buy comes later, at about DKK 13,000-15,500 a share

Share price DKK 19,895 (11 November 2026), about USD 2,948 at DKK 6.75 per USD; market value about USD 43bn. Money is in USD unless stated. An FFE (forty-foot equivalent unit) is the container measure in which Maersk reports volume and freight rates; a TEU (twenty-foot equivalent unit) is half of one FFE. Sources and the basis of the figures are in the end notes.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one paragraph. Maersk's earnings come down to one number multiplied by a very large volume: the average freight rate Maersk earns on about 13.6m loaded containers (FFE) a year. Maersk's average freight rate peaked in the third quarter of 2026 because ships were tied up on longer routes round Africa and in port queues. Both of those absorbers of capacity are now releasing ships just as the largest wave of new-ship deliveries the industry has ever contracted begins. The direction of Maersk's earnings over the next 12 to 24 months is therefore about as predictable as a forecast gets, and the direction is down; the level of those earnings is not predictable at all. The shares have priced the turn in earnings but not the trough. Maersk is not one of Richard's Target Setups today. Maersk is likely to become one, and this memo sets out when, and what to watch.

The insights that matter most

  1. The 2026 tailwind was rented; the headwind is contracted. The 2026 peak in freight rates came from capacity absorption (ships diverted away from the Red Sea, and port congestion), not from demand. That absorption is unwinding in plain sight, and the new ships that will replace the absorbed capacity are ordered, financed and dated.
  2. Maersk's earnings gearing to the freight rate is extreme and works in both directions. USD 100 per FFE on the annual freight rate is about USD 1.4bn of EBITDA and nearly USD 100 of EPS, against base-case EPS of USD 89 for 2027. The base-case freight rate for 2028 is only USD 10 per FFE above the rate at which group operating profit is nil.
  3. The market already agrees on the direction, so surprises are skewed against a buyer. Only 7% of brokers rate the shares a Buy. Guidance for 2026 equals consensus, and there is no guidance beyond 2026. What the shares do not yet reflect is the depth and duration of the trough: Viewforth's forecasts sit in the lowest broker camp, at about half the consensus EPS for 2027, and show a loss in 2028 where consensus has a profit. I can find no unrecognised positive within 18 months.
  4. The outlook has two regimes, not one bell curve. About 80-85% of the probability is continued normalisation of shipping routes, with a modest downward lean inside it; 15-20% is a new closure of the Red Sea or the Strait of Hormuz, which would lift every carrier's earnings within weeks. The most likely forecast error is small and negative; the largest possible error is large and positive.
  5. Maersk's strengths survive the trough but do not change its direction. APM Terminals (a real moat), a net cash balance sheet and the Gemini network (designed for loose markets) mean Maersk survives the trough comfortably and pays a dividend worth about 7% of today's price in March 2027. These strengths set the floor under the shares; they do not change the direction of earnings.
  6. A price-to-earnings multiple cannot value the trough; three other anchors can. A price-to-earnings multiple applied to trough losses gives a meaningless answer (the model's 18-month return is below -100%). Three independent anchors (0.45-0.5 times book value, the guideline multiple applied to through-cycle earnings, and the group valued with Ocean at nil) all point to roughly DKK 13,000-15,500 a share, a quarter to a third below today's price.
  7. The same gearing works in reverse from the trough, and that is the setup to wait for. From the trough freight rate, a rise of USD 200 per FFE adds about USD 200 of EPS with no extra capital. A trough-on-trough entry, at about 0.4-0.5 times book value with losses in consensus and scrapping under way, is the setup worth waiting for. The markers of that setup are observable, and none is present yet.
The five judgements that move the value of the shares (worked through, with the arithmetic, in #9): the pace of the freight-rate fall in 2027; the depth and length of the trough in 2028-2029; how much of the 2026 cost inflation reverses; whether a new closure of a shipping route occurs; and the multiple of book value the market pays at the trough, and the book value it pays that multiple on.
11Feb 2027
The next test is 11 February 2027, when Maersk publishes its fourth-quarter results, its first 2027 guidance, the dividend, the buyback decision and the annual report, all on one day.

#1 Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

Conclusion: The external tailwind behind Maersk's 2026 peak is temporary and visibly fading, while the headwind of new-ship deliveries is contracted and peaks in 2028, so the operating environment is strongly negative for the next 12 to 24 months; only one unforecastable event, a new closure of a shipping route, could reverse it.

Evidence

  • What made the 2026 peak. Routing ships round the Cape of Good Hope, to avoid the Red Sea, tied up about 7% of the world container fleet, and port queues tied up a further 11-12.6% at their August-September high. Demand grew at its usual 2-4% a year.
  • Both absorbers of capacity are releasing ships. Suez Canal containership transits were back to 73% of their 2023 level in the week to 6 November 2026. Services carrying 63% of Far East-Europe capacity already use the canal; Evergreen, one of the holdouts, has returned; and Hapag-Lloyd says its own return frees the equivalent of ten large ships. Waiting times at Shanghai are falling.
  • The new supply is contracted. The orderbook of new ships is 44% of the existing fleet. Bernstein has the fleet growing 7.4% in 2027 and 13.2% in 2028. Measured in ship-miles, demand falls 0.7% in 2027 (Deutsche Bank), because the shorter routes through Suez need fewer ship-miles. Scrapping is about 43,000 TEU this year on a fleet of 34m TEU, and idle capacity is between 1% and 2.5% of the fleet, depending on the measure.
  • Customers are already acting on the expected fall in freight rates. 79% of shippers surveyed hold all the peak-season stock they need; cargo owners are delaying the signature of 2027 contracts; and Xeneta, a freight-rate data provider, projects spot rates 30% lower in 2027.
  • Costs lean the same way. Fuel was 25% dearer in the third quarter of 2026; the EU carbon bill rises toward USD 0.5bn a year by 2027; and Maersk has chartered ships for five to seven years at peak charter rates.

Inference. Demand growth is a second-order variable: with supply growing 7-13% a year, the difference between 2% and 4% demand growth does not change the answer. The return of container shipping through Suez is now an observed process, not a forecast, so the "disruption continues" outcome needs a new closure that reverses a return already in progress. I put a probability of 15-20% on a new closure within a year.

So what. The operating environment sets the shape of the freight-rate path: a fast fall through the first half of 2027 (first the return through Suez, then the annual contract season), and a long trough through 2028 and 2029. About 3.6m TEU of new ships, a further 9.7% of the fleet, is still scheduled for delivery in 2029 (Jefferies), so 2029 is a second trough year, not the start of a recovery.

Strongest counter-case. Management, Jefferies and several Asian carriers argue that bottlenecks on land have decoupled ship capacity from transport capacity, so port queues will absorb the new ships. Charter rates rose in every ship-size class in October 2026, and forecasts of normalisation proved early in 2024, 2025 and 2026. The port data argue against the counter-case: terminal utilisation outside China is 58-70% and falling, a record 58m TEU of new terminal capacity opens in 2026, and utilisation at Maersk's own terminals fell to 85%. Port congestion is Chinese, seasonal and weather-driven, which makes it episodic rather than structural.

What would change my view. Freight rates holding through the first and second quarters of 2027 with Suez transits above 90% of 2023 levels, which would show that the new ships are being absorbed on land; a new closure; or, for the timing of recovery, idle capacity above 4% of the fleet and scrapping above 1% of the fleet a year.

Versus the market. I agree with the market on the direction of freight rates, which every covering broker states. I differ on the pace: most broker notes describe a gradual return through Suez over 2027, whereas the transit counts say the return is nearly done. I also differ on 2029: the delivery data are in the brokers' notes, but the conclusion that 2029 is a second trough year is not in their numbers.

Score: 12, set by the Rater. The 2026 peak came from rented capacity absorption (the Cape diversion tying up about 7% of the fleet, port queues another 11-12%) that is visibly releasing (Suez transits at 73% of 2023 and rising), into a contracted supply wave (orderbook 44% of the fleet, fleet growth 7.4% in 2027 and 13.2% in 2028, a further 9.7% in 2029), with distance-adjusted demand falling, shippers delaying contracts and fuel, EU carbon and peak-priced charters adding cost; revenue is forecast to fall 13% and EBITDA 42% in 2027. The headwind is contracted and still building into 2028-2029, with only an unforecastable new closure able to reverse it, so it is stronger than Yara's reversing scarcity price and level with Fugro's collapsed end market, coherent with the group's 12.

#2 Internally driven change

Conclusion: Maersk's internal change is real and competently executed but about a tenth the size of the freight-rate cycle, and its newest element, a fleet order at peak prices, weakens the case.

Evidence

Working. Gemini, the hub-and-spoke network Maersk has run with Hapag-Lloyd since February 2025, delivered USD 950m of benefits against a target of USD 820m to 1.1bn. About 1,000 corporate roles are being cut, worth about USD 0.18bn a year. The chief financial officer (in post since February 2026) and the head of Solutions both come from the freight forwarder Kuehne + Nagel. A USD 3bn programme adds about 30% to APM Terminals' capacity. The Logistics & Services margin has risen for nine consecutive quarters, to 5.8%.

Not working under stress. The Gemini network failed its first congested peak. In the third quarter of 2026 unit cost at constant fuel prices rose 5%, Maersk's volume fell 1% in a market growing 2-4%, and schedule reliability dropped from about 90% to between 68% and 80%, depending on the source.

Pointing the wrong way. In September 2026 Maersk ordered 26 ships of 18,600 TEU each for delivery in 2029-2030, about a tenth of its fleet, and dropped without explanation the fleet-size cap it had defended for years. Capital commitments rose from USD 13.4bn to 19.5bn in nine months. Maersk's share of world capacity, about 13.7%, is the lowest in twenty years. From January 2026 Maersk extended the accounting life of its vessels from 20 to 25 years, which adds about USD 0.7bn a year to operating profit and nothing to cash.

Inference

  1. Size. Everything management has said it will deliver (cost programmes, Terminals growth and a higher Logistics margin) adds up over four years to the value of USD 115 per FFE of freight rate. Maersk's realised freight rate moved by more than USD 500 per FFE in each of the last two quarters.
  2. Design. Gemini is a network built for loose markets. Gemini's cost edge showed when hubs were uncongested (unit cost fell 7% in the first quarter of 2026, the last loose quarter) and vanished when the hubs clogged. Gemini's performance should therefore look better in 2027 than in the third quarter of 2026, at exactly the time the freight rate is falling.
  3. Direction. Management's largest new decision is to defend market share by ordering ships at peak shipyard prices. The capital-discipline argument for preferring Maersk to other carriers has gone.

So what. Self-help (USD 0.6bn of EBITDA in 2027 and 1.0bn by 2028 in the model) improves Maersk's rank among carriers at the trough and keeps Ocean cash-positive. Self-help does not change the sign or the timing of the trough. Because Maersk's investment is fixed while its earnings fall, Maersk's cash pile becomes the shock absorber (#5).

Strongest counter-case. The new chief financial officer, from a capital-light and family-controlled business, could reset the capital framework with a stated return hurdle, a capacity target and a buyback sized against the cycle. The controlling owner has separated businesses before (oil in 2017, drilling in 2019, towage in 2024), and APM Terminals is the obvious candidate for a separation; Morgan Stanley puts the conglomerate discount on Terminals at USD 14bn, a third of Maersk's market value. Losses from late 2027 would also trigger a larger cost programme of the 2023 kind, worth a further USD 0.3-0.4bn.

What would change my view. A capacity and return framework with numbers in it; deferral of part of the ship order; a buyback increased into share-price weakness; or APM Terminals financed or reported as a separate entity.

Versus the market. I agree with the market, which has discussed the ship order and the capital commitments prominently since September 2026. In one respect I am kinder than the bears: I expect most of the 2026 congestion cost to reverse, whereas DNB Carnegie and Morgan Stanley assume costs stay sticky.

Score: 43, set by the Rater. Real, funded self-help is working (Gemini delivered USD 950m of benefits against an 820m-1.1bn target, about 1,000 roles cut, a USD 3bn Terminals expansion, nine quarters of rising Logistics margin, 0.6-1.0bn of EBITDA in the model) but is about a tenth the size of the cycle, the network failed its first congested peak (unit cost +5%, volume -1% in a growing market, reliability down to 68-80%), share has fallen to a twenty-year low and the newest decision, 26 ships ordered at peak yard prices after dropping the fleet cap, plus the vessel-life change that adds 0.7bn of profit and no cash, point the wrong way. A mild net negative, a little below Indus Holding's externally driven gains and above Xvivo's execution problems, close to the group's 42.

#3 Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Conclusion: Maersk has a first-rate terminals business, a fortress balance sheet and capable operators inside an industry that does not allow Maersk's largest segment, Ocean, to earn its cost of capital, so Maersk's foundations are sturdy for survival and weak for returns.

Evidence

  • Industry. Container shipping is concentrated in form (the top five carriers hold about 65% of capacity) but behaves like a commodity market. The carriers that set prices put volume first and are not run for listed-equity returns: MSC (private, 21.5% share, the largest orderbook), CMA CGM (family-owned) and COSCO (state-owned). The industry holds net cash of USD 26-30bn, and the natural candidate for exit, ZIM, is being bought by Hapag-Lloyd. Entry is hard and exit is harder, so capacity stays in the market through losses. Value is captured upstream by shipyards (full to 2029) and ship-charter owners, and downstream by terminals and freight forwarders. Forwarders control up to half of ocean volume and increasingly treat Maersk, which aims to be an integrated logistics provider, as a competitor.
  • Competitive advantage. Maersk has one strong and widening moat: APM Terminals, with a return on invested capital (ROIC) of 13.8-16% against a 9% hurdle, indexed concessions averaging about 22 years, and 63% of revenue from other carriers; Hapag-Lloyd has just bought 25% of APM Terminals' Rotterdam hub. Maersk has one moderate advantage, which it shares with Hapag-Lloyd and which holds only when hubs are uncongested: Gemini's unit cost, 3-7% below that of non-Gemini carriers. Maersk has no advantage in price: its realised freight rate follows the spot indices at about 0.4-0.5 of their move with a lag of a quarter, and customers refused to pay a premium for green shipping.
  • Financial profile. Group ROIC was 5.7% in 2025 against a through-cycle target above 7.5% (Hapag-Lloyd earned 4.6% against a cost of capital of 9.4%). More than USD 8bn of logistics acquisitions since 2019 earn less than their cost of capital. The balance sheet is excellent: net cash excluding leases was about USD 15.5-16bn at the end of 2025, with credit ratings of BBB+ and Baa1.
  • Management. Maersk's management is a strong operator (Gemini was built on time; cost programmes were delivered in 2016 and 2023; the in-year guidance range has never been cut under the current chief executive) and a weak allocator of capital (the logistics acquisitions; a USD 10.9bn dividend and buybacks paid out at peaks; the buyback suspended at the 2024 low; ships ordered at the top). The controlling family holds about 66% of the votes. The long-term incentive plan puts 80% of its weight on segment returns on capital and none on EPS or shareholder return, and no executive has bought shares in the market.

Inference. The industry structure gives Maersk survival, not returns. The quality sits in APM Terminals, the part of the group that is 15% of this year's EBITDA and more than a third of trough EBITDA. Maersk is therefore not a quality cyclical: Maersk is a quality infrastructure asset and a fortress balance sheet wrapped around a commodity container carrier.

So what

  • The industry structure gives no support to freight rates in 2027-2028, and there is no weak carrier whose failure would end a price war early. The industry's balancing mechanism is the idling and scrapping of ships, which works more slowly, and that slow mechanism is why the trough is long.
  • Solvency is not in the range of outcomes, and the non-Ocean EBITDA floor (about USD 4.3bn in 2028) is higher than in the troughs of 2016 and 2023.
  • Outside shareholders cannot force better capital allocation; change comes on the controlling owner's timetable.

Strongest counter-case. Consolidation (the top ten carriers have gone from about 65% to about 85% of capacity since 2015) and the alliances could at last produce discipline: carriers cancelled sailings quickly in 2023, and the 2023 trough was short. APM Terminals alone is worth about DKK 10,800 a share on DNB Carnegie's sum-of-the-parts valuation, more than half the share price.

What would change my view. A margin-first statement from MSC or CMA CGM backed by the idling of ships; order deferrals across the industry; and, for Maersk, management incentives tied to per-share value.

Versus the market. I agree with the market. Bernstein values Ocean as a business that destroys value over the cycle. Brokers value APM Terminals separately but name no catalyst for a separation, and neither do I.

Score: 28, set by the Rater. APM Terminals is a genuine, widening moat (ROIC 13.8-16% against a 9% hurdle, 22-year concessions) and the balance sheet is a fortress (net cash about USD 15.5-16bn, BBB+), but the industry is a commodity in behaviour with volume-first private and state price-setters, value captured by yards, charter owners, terminals and forwarders, Ocean a price-taker with only a shared 3-7% Gemini cost edge, management a strong operator but pro-cyclical allocator, and earnings almost unpredictable. The figures tell the truth (ROIC 3.8%, 28th percentile; group 5.7% in 2025 against a 7.5% target; USD 8bn of logistics deals below their cost of capital); a price-taker below its cost of capital through the cycle, just below Instalco and above Hilton Food, coherent with the groups' 20/32/20/38.

#4 Guidance: conservatism and track record

Conclusion: Maersk's guidance is conservative in habit but follows the freight rate, so with consensus near the top of a large upgrade cycle the next guidance event is more likely to reset expectations down than to be beaten in any way that matters.

Evidence

  • The record of raises. Maersk raised its 2026 EBITDA guidance three times in five months, from a midpoint of USD 5.75bn in February to 14.25bn on 5 November. Each raise marked the range to the prevailing spot freight rate. Maersk also raised its range four times in 2024 and at least once in 2025.
  • The record of first ranges. Maersk's first annual range was below consensus in 2019, 2020, 2023 and 2024, each a year that followed strength, and in line with consensus in 2025 and 2026, after the bears had already cut their estimates. Consensus EPS for 2027 has risen about six-fold in three months.
  • The record of outcomes. In years without a new disruption, the outcome beat the midpoint of the first range by 2% to 50%. The two very large beats (246% in 2024 and 148% in 2026) each followed a new closure of a shipping route.
  • The market's reaction (figure below). The 5 November 2026 raise was the first raise the shares did not reward: the shares fell about 10% during the day, as third-quarter EBITDA missed consensus by 14% in a quarter when the freight rate rose 46%, the first miss of this cycle.
  • Today. The 2026 range (EBITDA of USD 14.0-14.5bn) brackets consensus. There is no guidance for 2027.

Inference. Maersk's guidance is honest and conservative in form, but it is a thermometer of the freight rate, so its conservatism pays the holder only when the freight rate surprises upward. For 11 February 2027 I put a probability of about 75% on a first 2027 EBITDA range whose midpoint is more than 5% below consensus, most likely a range of about USD 6-9bn. Once set low, the 2027 range is more likely to be raised (about 50%) than cut (about 22%) during 2027, even in the base case, in which quarterly EBITDA falls from about USD 3.1bn to about 1.3bn through the year.

So what. Richard's test (conservative guidance and a record of raising it) is met in form and failed in substance. A "guidance raised" headline in 2027 would say nothing about the business, and the share-price reaction to guidance is now asymmetric. The one number in the 11 February package that I hold with high confidence is the dividend, about USD 200 a share (about DKK 1,350), because Maersk's dividend policy is mechanical. On the buyback I expect a USD 1bn programme (about 60% probability of some programme); Morgan Stanley says consensus models USD 2bn, so the likelier surprise on the buyback is a smaller size.

Strongest counter-case. A low first range could be the clearing event: consensus is cut to the range in February, and Maersk then beats and raises through 2027 from a base nobody fears. A range of USD 7-10bn would be read as relief.

What would change my view. A midpoint at or above USD 8.5bn with the freight-rate assumption stated; a USD 2bn buyback; or an in-year raise that coincides with a rising quarterly freight rate.

Versus the market. The market expects a conservative first range, and Bernstein says so explicitly. The surprise will be in the level: the base case is consistent with a midpoint about 17% below consensus.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. In form the record is good: the in-year range has never been cut under this chief executive, 2026 guidance was raised three times (5.75bn to 14.25bn midpoint), 2024's four times, and outcomes beat the first range's midpoint in every year; but every raise marked the range to the spot rate rather than to fundamental delivery, the third quarter missed consensus EBITDA by 14%, the ROIC target is missed, and the company let consensus 2027 EPS run up six-fold with no 2027 steer. Honest and rate-driven like Entra but with less sign of keeping the sell side conservative, so below Sdiptech and above Instalco's missed targets, above the Guidance group's 38 because the in-year record has not broken.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Conclusion: Maersk's business model has exceptional operating leverage and no pricing power, so revenue changes produce outsized profit changes in both directions, and over the next 12 to 24 months the direction is down.

Evidence

  • Operating leverage. The Ocean cost base is largely fixed per sailing. Between the first and third quarters of 2026, two-thirds of the added Ocean revenue became operating profit.
  • The cost per FFE does move, but by only about a third as much as the freight rate. Fuel, the Cape route and congestion inflated the cash cost per FFE in 2026, from about USD 1,770 in 2025 to about 2,190 in the third quarter of 2026. The model has the cash cost per FFE back at about 1,770 by 2028.
  • Break-evens. Ocean EBITDA is nil at a freight rate of about USD 1,770-1,800 per FFE, Ocean operating profit is nil at about 2,100-2,150, and group operating profit (with the Terminals and Logistics floor) is nil at about 1,910. The base-case freight rate for 2028 is 1,920.
  • Financial leverage. Maersk has no financial leverage in the usual sense, but investment plus lease payments (about USD 9bn a year) exceed EBITDA in 2028-2029, so net cash falls and interest income turns to a net cost (figure below).
  • Fixed charges below operating profit. Tax is about USD 0.48bn a year whatever the profit, because Ocean is taxed on its capacity and the land businesses on their profit; in 2016 Maersk paid USD 1.05bn of tax on a pre-tax loss. The share count, which fell 27% between 2019 and 2025, stops falling after 2027.
  • Feedback loops. Reinforcing loops: profits fund ship orders, which become deliveries; cash buffers delay scrapping; each carrier that returns to Suez gains a cost edge and forces the rest to follow; contracts are shortening, so spot rates reach the realised rate faster; and Maersk's own investment turns falling cash flow into falling interest income. Balancing loops: idling, slow steaming and scrapping, which on the timing of 2015-2016 engage four to six quarters after losses become widespread.

Inference. The machine Richard looks for, in which a change in revenue produces an outsized change in profit, exists at Maersk in extreme form and is running in reverse. Each layer of leverage amplifies the one above it: price on a fixed cost base, then fixed charges on a small operating profit, then a shrinking cash pile. The feedback loops make the fall fast and the trough long.

So what. The constructive point is the mirror image. From the trough, a rise of USD 200 per FFE adds about USD 2.8bn of EBITDA (200 on about 14.2m FFE) and about USD 200 of EPS, with no extra cost, capital or shares. The step-up in earnings power that Richard wants is on offer when the freight rate turns up from below break-even, not while the freight rate is turning down from a peak.

Strongest counter-case. The leverage could be worse than modelled if cost proves sticky (DNB Carnegie raised its unit-cost estimates after the third quarter), or milder if Maersk's contract book cushions the fall more than I assume.

What would change my view. Unit cost at constant bunker-fuel prices falling 3-6% year on year by mid-2027 would confirm the cost cushion; a rising contract share with longer durations would show a smaller sensitivity to spot rates.

Versus the market. The market understands the price leverage, but the median estimate under-models the fixed charges. Consensus pre-tax profit for 2028 is above consensus operating profit, which implies net financial income while Maersk's cash is being spent. Correcting the net financial items is worth USD 30-40 a share of EPS cuts that need no fall in the freight rate. That correction is not an edge over the informed bears, who already model it.

Score: 38, set by the Rater. The structure has extreme operating leverage (Ocean cost largely fixed per sailing, two-thirds of added revenue reaching operating profit in 2026, USD 100 per FFE worth about USD 1.4bn of EBITDA and nearly USD 100 of EPS, fixed tax and depreciation amplifying further), which on its own would score well above 50; but there is no pricing power (the realised rate follows spot at 0.4-0.5 of its move and green premiums were refused), cost moves only about a third as much as the rate, and the industry loop turns profits into ships, so the gearing works against the company as revenue falls 13% and EPS 82% in 2027 and earns below its cost of capital through the cycle. Placed between the levels' 25 (extreme gearing to a price it cannot set) and BP's 50, consistent with the Economic strength group's 20 being dragged down by the downturn.

Evidence and reading

  • Against the past. Average EBITDA for 2027-2030 is about USD 7.4bn, 29% below the 2023-2025 average, on revenue 6% higher. Average EPS over those four years is about USD 2. In two of those years, 2028 and 2029, operating profit is near break-even and EPS is a loss.
  • The floor. Terminals and Logistics & Services together earn about USD 4.1bn of EBITDA in 2027, rising to about 4.8bn by 2030; Ocean EBITDA falls from about 10.3bn in 2026 to about 2.1bn at the trough.
  • Cash. Free cash flow should beat the 2026 guidance of "above USD 3.0bn" comfortably, and is then negative in every year to 2030.
  • Quality of earnings. Every operating profit figure from 2026 onward contains the accounting benefit of the longer vessel lives (#2), which is larger than the operating profit of 2028 and 2029 combined.

Inference. Over the next four years taken as a whole there is no scope for double-digit growth, or for growth and margins above the past. There is scope for growth from the trough: EBITDA rises 26% in 2030, and the model's five-year average EPS (2026-2030) is about USD 100, which is the best measure of through-cycle earnings power that the available files offer.

So what. The earnings the market must value in 12 to 24 months are trough earnings, and their sign is not known. The shape of the trough, a plateau and not a V, matters as much as its depth, because four years of negative free cash flow is what consumes the optionality of Maersk's balance sheet.

Strongest counter-case. Brokers who agree on the direction still disagree on the shape. Bernstein, which rates the shares Underperform, has the freight rate stabilising near USD 2,240-2,290 per FFE and EBITDA rising from 9.8bn in 2027 to 11.65bn in 2029. DNB Carnegie has 2028 EBITDA at 4.0bn. The Viewforth base case sits between the two. Its floor assumptions (cost relief, Terminals flat in 2027, a Logistics margin of 5.5-5.8%) are each at the favourable end of their records, so I read the base-case 2028 EBITDA as nearer the 60th-65th percentile of outcomes within the base scenario than its middle. I have not changed those inputs, because the freight rate matters far more than these items; a weak 2028 would not be a surprise.

What would change my view. The thresholds in the dated tests in #7, above all the first- and second-quarter 2027 freight rates and unit cost.

Versus the market. The Ocean freight rate, the least knowable item in the case, explains about 60% of the gap between Viewforth's and consensus 2027 EPS and about 75% of the 2028 gap; the rest is mainly net financial items. (I measured the split by putting consensus EBITDA through Viewforth's own lines below EBITDA.) On operating profit, the model summary shows gaps of 37% in 2027 and 137% in 2028; on the company's basis, which includes joint ventures as consensus does, the gaps are about 22% and 80%.

Score: 5, set by the Rater. Falling earnings give F; the decline is organic and rate-driven, EBITDA margin troughs at 11.6% against 19.5% in 2023-2025, operating profit is near break-even for two years even with the vessel-life benefit, free cash flow is negative every year, and 2030 recovers only to a fraction of the past, so near the floor of the band.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6-12 months

Conclusion: Over the next 6-12 months Viewforth's forecasts point to cuts in consensus and a first 2027 guidance range below consensus, so the scope for upgrades is low and rests on a new disruption.

Evidence

  • Estimates form three camps, not one consensus. Of sixteen visible brokers, seven have 2027 EPS between USD 60 and 116, three between 185 and 211, and six between 259 and 451. Viewforth's 89 is inside the lowest camp. The consensus median falls when the highest camp gives way, and the highest camp's thesis (that port congestion absorbs the new ships) is tested only by falling reported freight rates.
  • Revisions are geared. Depreciation is fixed, so each 1% off consensus 2027 EBITDA is about USD 6 a share, or 3.3% of consensus EPS. A 10% cut to 2027 EBITDA is a 33% cut to 2027 EPS and takes 2028 EPS to about zero.
  • The odds favour cuts. I adopt the probabilities of the third and fourth sets of earlier analysis, shown in the second figure below.

The tests, in date order

Inference. The scope for Viewforth's forecasts to produce upgrades to guidance or consensus over 6-12 months is low, and the scope for cuts is high. The expected path of estimates is roughly flat to February 2027, cut after the first 2027 range, paused around a first-quarter result that still shows growth, and falling again from August 2027.

So what. The narrative moves from "when does the cycle turn?" to "how deep and how long is the trough?". The items the market has not yet added up become the debate: decaying interest income, the tax floor, the share of trough profit that comes from the longer accounting life of vessels, thin headroom in the impairment test, and a second trough year in 2029.

Four developments in 2027 will look like improvement and are not:

Two results that still show growthYear-on-year growth on a depressed base, while the freight rate is already falling.
A raised guidance rangeA raise from a low first range, while quarterly EBITDA halves.
Rating upgrades on valuationBrokers upgrade on a lower share price while their estimates fall.
2027 contract rates "up"Compatible with a realised rate a quarter below 2026's, because the 2026 contracts were struck at the low of early 2026.

Strongest counter-case. A new closure would take 2027 EBITDA to about USD 12-14bn and EPS to about USD 400-480, and would vindicate the highest camp. Short of a closure, a firm contract season could hold consensus EBITDA near USD 9bn until August 2027.

What would change my view. A fourth-quarter 2026 freight rate above USD 3,000 per FFE followed by a first-quarter 2027 rate above 2,900.

Versus the market. The sell side expects cuts, as its ratings show, but its numbers have not followed. My difference is one of timing and extent: the highest camp gives way by August 2027, and the fall in EPS will look far larger than the fall in EBITDA that causes it.

Score: 11, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is about 75% likely to start 2027 with a midpoint more than 5% below consensus (model consistent with about 17% below), consensus 2027 EPS of 188 sits about double the model's 89 with net revisions about 85% likely to be negative within twelve months and 2028 consensus about 55-60% likely to turn to a loss, and the narrative is moving to how deep and how long; with revenue falling the downgrade cannot be scaled to growth and is simply large. Only a 15-20% chance of a new closure, and later in-year raises off a low base, offer scope, so it sits below Yara's fading geopolitical windfall and above Bally's, in line with the fourth set's 18 shaded lower for the size of the likely cut.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price and peers

Conclusion: Maersk's momentum is strong on the measures that lag and has turned on the measures that lead, for Maersk and for its closest peer, so momentum is peaking, not building.

Evidence (dashboard ratings as pinned on 10-11 November 2026)

  • Sell-side momentum: B, down from A at the 8 November memo. Consensus 2027 EBITDA is up 7% in a month and 58% in three; the moves in EPS and the target price are in the figure on lagging and leading gauges below.
  • Technical momentum: A. The price is 14% below its 50-day average (DKK 23,051) but 5% above its 150-day average (DKK 18,916). The return is -3.9% over three months, against +50.9% over twelve.
  • Valuation: F. The price-to-earnings multiple is at the 100th percentile of its ten-year history.
  • Narrative. Good news has stopped being rewarded: the latest guidance raise was sold (#4).
  • Peers. Hapag-Lloyd, the closest peer, is rated D on technical momentum and is up 14% in twelve months; on 12 November it reported third-quarter EBITDA below consensus on the same cost pressures, and consensus has its operating margin at -1% three years out. The wider shipping group is still strong (NORDEN, CMB.TECH and Hoegh Autoliners are rated A on technical momentum). Evergreen and Wan Hai reported October revenue up about 8% on September, so the fourth quarter of 2026 is still good.

Inference. The gauges that lag (three-month revisions, the 200-day trend) are strong; the gauges that lead (the target price, 2028 estimates, the price against its 50-day average, the reaction to good news) have turned. Momentum and short-covering, not conviction, drove the 51% rise in the share price while only 7% of brokers rated the shares a Buy (short interest was a third of the free float in August 2025), and that fuel is now spent.

So what. Momentum no longer helps a holder, and it is not yet washed out. A close below the 150-day average, 5% below the price, would confirm the turn technically. The shares move with the freight indices and Red Sea headlines, by 10-20% in days, so a correct view of Maersk's own numbers does not make the share price predictable over six months.

Strongest counter-case. The long trend is intact; discretionary investors are already lightly positioned (Deutsche Bank, 6 November 2026); index inclusion and a dividend of about 7% lie ahead; and the next two results will show growth. Any Red Sea headline would squeeze rebuilt short positions again.

What would change my view. The price back above its 50-day average with spot freight indices rising, and 2028 estimates rising alongside 2027 estimates.

Versus the market. The dashboard's mechanical ratings say momentum is strong. I read those ratings as lagging, and the price action says the market does too.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. Both measures are in the top fifth, which would give A, but parts are negative: the narrative has turned (the 5 November raise was sold, the first miss of the cycle), the consensus target and 2028 EPS (-22% in a month) are falling, the price is 14% below its 50-day average and 22% off its high, and the closest peer Hapag-Lloyd is weak; guidance was raised and 2027 EPS is still up 20% in a month, so B, placed near the floor because the leading gauges have turned.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the case

Conclusion: The Maersk case is as simple as an investment case gets and among the riskiest, because one exogenous number, the freight rate, decides earnings; the freight rate has a history of moving USD 500 per FFE in a quarter, and each USD 100 per FFE is worth about a year of base-case EPS.

Evidence

  • Simple. One variable, the freight rate, generates about 160% of the fall in EBITDA from 2026 to 2028. Beneath the freight rate sit two root causes: a delivery schedule of new ships (contracted) and the Red Sea (political).
  • High-risk. The range of outcomes is wider than the base case itself. 2027 EBITDA is about USD 4.7bn in a deeper price war (about 30% probability), 8.2bn in the base case (about 50%) and 13.7bn after a new closure (about 20%, which the latest transit data argue for shading to 15%). 2027 EPS runs from about USD -160 to about +480, a span equal to about a fifth of the share price in one year's earnings. A loss per share in 2028 is about a two-in-three call.
  • Trackable. Spot freight indices and Suez transits are published weekly, and realised rates follow spot rates by about a quarter, so much of each result is knowable before Maersk reports it. Danish rules oblige the company to announce a material departure from guidance when it identifies one.
  • Sudden. Guidance days have moved the shares 10-17%, and a ceasefire or an attack moves every carrier's shares at once.
  • Precedent. The shares have followed the freight index, not reported earnings. The shares peaked within about two months of the freight index in 2015, 2022 and 2026. In 2015-2016 the shares fell 55% to 0.4-0.5 times book value and bottomed well before earnings did. In 2023-2024 the low on the dashboard's monthly series came with the February 2024 guidance shock, when a new closure was already lifting freight rates.
  • Book-value risk. Headroom in the Ocean impairment test was USD 1.1bn at the end of 2025, down from 4.1bn, and a rise of 0.2 percentage points in the discount rate would remove it. I put the probability of an impairment at about 30% at the February 2027 results and about 60% by February 2028.
  • Not at risk. Solvency, the investment-grade credit rating in the base case, and the March 2027 dividend.

The five judgements that move the value, with the arithmetic

1

1. The pace of the fall: the 2027 rate (base about 2,155 per FFE).

  • Each USD 100 on 13.6m FFE is USD 1.36bn of revenue with no cost attached, so USD 1.36bn of EBITDA and of operating profit.
  • Depreciation, interest and the tax floor do not move, and Ocean's marginal tax is close to nil, so net income moves by the same 1.36bn; on 14.18m shares that is USD 96 of EPS, more than the whole base-case figure.
  • Deeper case, about 1,860 (-295): 295 x 13.6m = 4.0bn, of which cost actions give back about 0.5bn, so EBITDA is about 4.7bn, EPS about -160 (89 less 3.5bn / 14.18m), free cash flow about -4.5bn against -1.0bn, and no dividend for 2027.
  • Closure case, about 2,600 (+445): EBITDA about 13.7bn, EPS about +480, free cash flow about +4bn, and a dividend of about USD 190 in place of 35.
2

2. The depth and length of the trough: the 2028 rate (base 1,920).

  • A plausible error is 150 either way (a 2019-like trough is about 2,100; a 2016-like one about 1,650).
  • 150 x 13.9m FFE = 2.1bn of EBITDA. Company-basis operating profit of 0.15bn becomes about +2.2bn or -1.9bn.
  • On 13.98m shares that is USD 149: EPS of -67 becomes about +82 or about -216.
  • Free cash flow of -3.5bn becomes about -1.4bn or about -5.5bn.
  • Length: if 2030 repeats 2029's rate in place of rising by 100, 100 x 14.7m = 1.47bn, or USD 105 a share; 2030 EPS of 43 becomes about -62 and a further 1.5bn of cash goes.
3

3. The cost cushion (base: cash cost per FFE falls from about 2,060 in 2026 to 1,770 in 2028).

  • About 220-250 of the fall from the third-quarter peak is non-fuel cost, which needs charters redelivered and congestion cleared. I put about 55% on the full relief arriving.
  • If a quarter of the non-fuel relief fails: 60 x 13.9m = 0.83bn of EBITDA, USD 60 a share; 2028 EPS becomes about -127 and free cash flow about -4.3bn.
  • Each further 1% on the Ocean cash cost (about 18 per FFE) is 0.25bn and USD 18 a share, in either direction.
4

4. No new closure (base: about 80-85% that normalisation continues).

  • If wrong, the figures are the closure case in judgement 1, and on my book-value cross-check the shares return about +45% over 18 months, against about -25% in the base.
  • Every five points of probability is therefore worth about 3.5 points of expected return (0.05 x 70).
5

5. The multiple of book value at the trough, and the book it is applied to (base cross-check: 0.45-0.5 times a book value of about USD 4,185 a share at the end of 2027).

  • Each 0.05 of multiple is 0.05 x 4,185 x 6.75 = DKK 1,412, or 7% of today's price.
  • At 0.4 times, about DKK 11,300 (-43% in price); at 0.5 times, about DKK 14,100 (-29%); at 0.6 times, about DKK 16,950 (-15%).
  • An impairment of USD 3bn takes about USD 214 a share off book (3bn / 14.0m), which at 0.45 times is about DKK 650, or 3% of the price; it also lowers depreciation by about 0.2bn, adding about USD 14 to EPS.

Inference. The case is simple to state and to follow, and it is high-risk, because the error in the forecast is the error in one number, the freight rate, multiplied by about 14m FFE. Three fragilities sit inside the base case:

  1. The cost relief is assumed, not observed. Both earlier sets of analysis assume the cost relief, and no broker models it explicitly.
  2. The freight-rate floor may not hold. The base case assumes the price-setting carriers stop cutting at the marginal carrier's cash cost, which in 2016 they did not do until a carrier failed.
  3. Volume and freight rate are one assumption, not two. The volume assumption (growth of 2.5% in 2027 while Maersk loses market share) holds only if Maersk fills its freed ships by cutting price.

So what. Treat the base case as the most likely path, checked against dated tests, not as the middle of a symmetrical range. Position size, more than conviction about the level of earnings, is the tool for managing a case like Maersk.

Strongest counter-case. The risk is two-sided, and the upside arrives faster: a closure re-rates all carriers within weeks, and the bears have been early three years running.

What would change my view. Evidence that the range of outcomes is narrowing: a larger and longer contract book, or industry discipline (the idling of ships) appearing before losses.

Versus the market. I agree with the market, which knows how wide the range is: Morgan Stanley's twelve-month bull and bear values are DKK 36,400 and DKK 10,000.

Score: 15, set by the Rater. The case is simple and trackable (one variable makes about 160% of the 2026-2028 EBITDA fall, spot and Suez data are weekly, realised rates lag spot by a quarter) and net cash keeps solvency and the March dividend out of the range, but the range for 2027 EPS runs from about -160 to +480 around a base of 89 in two regimes, the sign of 2028 EPS is a two-in-three call for a loss, guidance days move the shares 10-17% and a headline moves every carrier at once, with an Ocean impairment about 60% likely by 2028. Wider and more binary than Instalco's roll-up but without Teqnion's irregularities or Hexatronic's leverage, near the Risks groups' 22 and 28 shaded down for the two-regime cone.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: Maersk is past the peak of its Reinforcing phase and stalling, with a collapse in estimate momentum the likely next step and a bottom not before 2028.

Evidence. The dashboard's rule places Maersk in the Reinforcing phase. Six facts argue against that placement: the latest guidance raise was sold; the third quarter missed consensus; the price has broken below its 50-day average; the consensus target price has started to fall; 2028 estimates are falling while 2027 estimates are still being marked up; and the input that drove the phase, the spot freight rate, has rolled over while Suez transits rise.

Inference. Maersk is past the top of the Reinforcing phase and stalling. In the base case the next phase is a collapse of estimate momentum through 2027, and bottoming is a 2028 event at the earliest.

So what: the markers of the next opportunity. None of the four markers is present today, and all four are observable.

The buying window is likely to open before the earnings low. The share price has bottomed before reported earnings, and in the last cycle it bottomed on a guidance shock. If earnings trough in 2028-2029, the window is more likely to open between late 2027 and the first 2028 guidance range in February 2028 than at the earnings low. February 2027 is too early, because trough freight rates will not yet be visible.

Strongest counter-case. A new closure would extend the Reinforcing phase by two to four quarters, as closures did in December 2023 and again in 2026. A closure would delay the trough, not cancel the delivery wave.

What would change my view. Freight rates holding into mid-2027 with Suez fully open (back to Reinforcing), or the four markers above appearing early (forward to bottoming).

Versus the market. The dashboard's mechanical rule says Reinforcing. The price, and broker ratings that carry rising numbers but no Buy calls, say the market already treats the stock as stalling. I agree with the market.

Score: 21, set by the Rater. The computed Reinforcing is wrong: the guidance raise was sold, the third quarter missed, the price has broken its 50-day average, the target price and 2028 estimates are falling while 2027's are still marked up, and the spot rate driving the phase has rolled over with Suez transits rising, so the stock is past the top and stalling, with a collapse in estimate momentum the likely next step through 2027 and bottoming not before 2028. Later than Imperial Brands' ex-growth stall because the collapse is dated and near, but not yet Judges Scientific's realised collapse because consensus and reported growth have not yet turned.

#11 The fair multiple

Conclusion: The guideline's 22.0 times is generous for a stalling stock and cannot be applied to negative trough earnings, but applied to through-cycle earnings it lands where book value does, at roughly DKK 13,000-15,500 a share.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for Maersk is 22.0 times two-year-forward earnings, the 90th percentile of the stock's ten-year range (10th percentile 10.2 times, median 15.0, 75th percentile 18.3), because the dashboard's rule places the stock in the Reinforcing phase. The multiple today is 92.5 times on consensus earnings, and negative on the model's forecasts.

My view of the guideline multiple, in three parts

  1. On phase, the guideline is generous. I judge the stock to be stalling (#10), and the framework gives a stalling stock a lower place in its range. The median of 15 times would be the more natural reference.
  2. The ten-year range is an unreliable ruler for a deep cyclical such as Maersk, because the range runs backwards. The dashboard's own history shows this. At the 2021-2022 earnings peak, the height of delivery, the market paid 6-8 times, below the 10th percentile. From late 2023 into 2025, when the earnings expected two years out were at their lowest, the multiple was 90-150 times or not meaningful. For Maersk a high multiple marks low expected earnings, not high esteem, so the rule "higher in the range for peak delivery" gives the wrong sign.
  3. The guideline is usable on through-cycle earnings, and then it agrees with the other anchors. On the model's five-year average EPS of about USD 100, 22 times is about DKK 14,900 a share and the median of 15 times about DKK 10,100. Book value gives DKK 12,700-14,100 at the 0.45-0.5 times of past troughs. The sum of the parts with Ocean at nil gives about DKK 14,000-15,700. The three methods meet at roughly DKK 13,000-15,500. One caution applies: a multiple of "normal" earnings is a freight-rate forecast in disguise, since each USD 50 of normal EPS is about DKK 7,400 a share at 22 times.

So what. I accept 22.0 times as the figure #12 uses. Applied to two-year-forward earnings, 22 times cannot value Maersk in the next 18 months, because those earnings are negative. Applied to through-cycle earnings, 22 times says the same as book value: fair value is below the price, and the level at which the shares stop depending on the freight rate being right is about a quarter to a third below today's price.

Strongest counter-case. A higher multiple could be earned through a separation of APM Terminals, which would attract an infrastructure multiple, or by a market that looks through the trough to recovery, as the market did at about 0.5 times book in 2023-2024.

What would change my view. A sponsor for the separation of APM Terminals, or evidence of industry scrapping that shortens the trough.

Versus the market. The market's working multiple is about 0.7 times book value: Morgan Stanley uses exactly that multiple in its target, and the consensus target equals the price. A multiple of 0.7 times is mid-range for a stock heading into a trough, and history says troughs are priced at 0.4-0.5 times.

Score: 14, set by the Rater. Dear on both gives F; both readings are inflated by near-zero two-year-forward earnings, which would lift the number, but on the memo's book-value yardstick the shares at about 0.7 times book still sit well above the 0.4-0.5 times at which a stalling stock heading into a trough has been priced, so the dearness is largely real and the number stays low in the band.

#12 Total shareholder return

Conclusion: The model's return at the guideline multiple is deeply negative because a peak-phase multiple meets trough earnings; on a book-value cross-check the 18-month return is still about -20% to -30% in the base case, with dividends of 8% the only positive component.

The model's figures (at the guideline multiple of 22.0 times, from a price of DKK 19,785)

Horizon Total return Annualised Value per share From dividends From the multiple From earnings
The 18-month column, to 31 March 2028 -115.6% n/a DKK -3,086 +8.0% not shown not shown
The three-year column, to 30 September 2029 -57.9% -25.9% DKK 8,324 +8.0% not shown not shown

The model does not split the change in price between the multiple and earnings, because today's multiple on the model's own forecasts is negative (-42.8 times), and a change from a negative multiple has no meaning. The three paragraphs below are my reconstruction of what drives each figure.

Dividends: +8.0%, all of it by March 2028. USD 200 a share for 2026 (paid March 2027) and USD 35 for 2027 (paid March 2028) make USD 235, about DKK 1,586. Nothing follows, because a loss year pays no dividend under the policy.

Earnings and the multiple at 18 months: an artefact. The earnings to which the multiple is applied at 31 March 2028 are those of the year to March 2030, about USD -31 a share (three-quarters of 2029's -56 plus a quarter of 2030's +43). Twenty-two times a loss is a negative share price, about DKK -4,670; adding the dividends gives DKK -3,086. The -115.6% measures how unsuitable a price-to-earnings multiple is at a cyclical trough. It is not an expected loss.

Earnings and the multiple at three years: the earnings shortfall. The value implies two-year-forward EPS of about USD 45 (for the year to September 2031); 22 times that EPS is about DKK 6,740, and the dividends bring the value to DKK 8,324. There are two ways to read the 66% fall in price:

  • Holding the multiple at 22 times throughout, today's price capitalises about USD 133 of two-year-forward EPS (19,785 / 6.75 / 22). The model has about USD 45. The whole fall in price is that earnings shortfall.
  • On the dashboard's consensus basis, the multiple falls from 92.5 to 22 times (-76%) while two-year-forward EPS rises from about USD 32 to about USD 45 (+42%); the two changes multiply to about -66%. The guideline assumes that a trough multiple comes down to a peak-phase multiple while earnings are still near the trough.

Both readings point to the same driver: at the guideline multiple, today's price needs about USD 133 of two-year-forward EPS, a third above the model's through-cycle average of about USD 100 and above the two brokers' 2029 consensus of USD 115.

My own cross-check, on book value (not model figures)

  • 18 months. Base case: 0.45-0.5 times a book value of about USD 4,185 a share, less a likely impairment, is about DKK 12,100-14,100 a share; with the dividends, that is a total return of about -20% to -30%. The deeper case gives about -40%, and the closure case about +45%. Weighted by the scenario probabilities, the return is about -15% to -20%.
  • Three years. On a book value of about USD 3,850-4,050 a share: if the trough multiple of 0.45-0.5 times still holds in late 2029, the return is about -25% to -35%; if recovery is in sight and the shares trade on 0.6-0.8 times book, about -15% to +15%. The model's -57.9% probably overstates the three-year loss, because at past troughs the market has priced Maersk on book value, not on depressed earnings.

So what. In the next 18 months the return is the 8% from dividends set against a de-rating from about 0.7 times book value toward the trough range of 0.4-0.5 times, on a book value that is itself shrinking a little. The return from earnings growth and re-rating is real, but it belongs to a buyer at the trough, not to a holder through it.

Strongest counter-case. The closure case; a market that pays for the recovery early; or a separation of APM Terminals, which would move value without moving earnings.

What would change my view. The four markers in #10. From about DKK 13,000-15,500 a share, with those markers present, the same arithmetic gives a strongly positive three-year return.

Versus the market. With the consensus target at the share price, the market expects a total return of about the dividend. My difference is that I expect the multiple of book value to complete its journey to the trough range.

Score: 10, set by the Rater. A loss gives F, and -15% to -20% maps to about 10-12 on the scale; the base case is -20% to -30% with dividends of 8% the only positive, the deeper case -40%, and the upper tail (+45% on a closure) is fat but unforecastable, so placed at 10.

#13 Summary conclusion

Maersk is a well-run operator with a first-rate terminals business and a fortress balance sheet, whose earnings are decided by a freight rate it does not control. The freight rate has peaked for reasons that are reversing in public view, into a supply wave that is contracted. The market knows the direction of earnings but has not yet priced the depth or the length of the trough. Guidance, estimates and the narrative are all more likely to move down than up over the next year, and the price sits half-way between the peak and trough multiples of book value. Nothing in the case is skewed to the positive today, except through a new closure that nobody can forecast.

The energising part is what comes next. The gearing that takes EPS from about USD 490 to a loss works just as hard in the other direction, the balance sheet guarantees that Maersk survives to benefit, and the signs of the turn (idling, scrapping, an impairment taken, losses in consensus, shares at about 0.4-0.5 times book) can be tracked week by week. The work now is to watch the dated tests, starting on 11 February 2027, and to be ready with a view of book value and trough earnings when the shares reach the DKK 13,000-15,500 zone.

Foundations' Robustness: 32, set by the Rater. Setups' Fit/Crispness: 8, set by the Rater. The memo finds no Target Setup fits today; the nearest, a quality cyclical at trough-on-trough with the cause for concern clearing, is contradicted in substance because the cause for concern is arriving rather than clearing and only the Terminals part of the group is quality, so the case is the inverse of that setup (a windfall at the point the setup would sell).

Case Riskiness: 17, set by the Rater. Simple and trackable, with net cash keeping balance-sheet risk out, but one exogenous freight rate in a two-regime cone decides earnings (2027 EPS -160 to +480, 2028 sign uncertain) with sudden 10-20% share moves (topic 9 at 15); the simplicity and solvency hold it just above topic 9 and above the levels' 10, which need leverage that turns a miss into a balance-sheet problem.

End notes

  • Basis of the figures. The share price is DKK 19,895 on 11 November 2026; the Financial Analyst's model uses DKK 19,785. Forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model, update 2, base case, and I change no forecast input. Consensus is the FactSet median at 11 November 2026 unless a figure is marked as a mean. EBITDA and EPS are on the company's "underlying" basis, which is the brokers' basis.
  • References to the "second", "third" and "fourth sets" are to the earlier sets of analysis on which this memo draws. The balance-sheet path in #5 is the second set's, on the company's basis; the revision probabilities in #7 are the third and fourth sets'.
  • Default charts and tables are from FactSet, the Master Dashboard and the one-page summary of the Financial Analyst's model, as noted under each; library charts were drawn from the figures in the memo text.
  • Consensus is shown by named financial year throughout; where a consensus figure covers only two brokers, the memo says so.
  • The co-movement of Maersk's shares with the freight indices and Red Sea headlines (#8) cannot be quantified, because the table supplied for it is empty.
  • Requests for the model (#12). The Financial Analyst should show, alongside the return at the guideline multiple, the same return on a price-to-book or through-cycle-earnings basis whenever two-year-forward EPS is negative, so that the return of record is interpretable. The Financial Analyst should also reconcile the model's year-end net cash line: the line opens 2026 at USD -3.7bn with an unexplained difference of 4.4bn inside the reported quarters, whereas the company reported net cash including leases of 3.2bn at the third quarter. For the balance sheet I have used the second set's company-basis path.
  • Grades: A 90 to 100, B 75 to 89, C 50 to 74, D 25 to 49, F 1 to 24.

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

  • Consensus net income for FY2026 is 7,407.00, +224.9% against 2,280.00 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +20.5%.
  • Consensus earnings per share for FY2026 is 507.23, +226.3% against 155.45 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +20.5%.

Facts in the data file that commonly explain such a gap:

  • Hybrid bond coupons and capitalised leases are not in the data file; check the company's reporting where relevant.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
